note:
v1, ON ITS HINGE (track eleven, drawn empty; whole-song skeleton). One B-flat guitar riff that a drummer can walk through two ways: six quick steps at 144 or four broad ones at 96 in the same twelve eighths. The tempo map does not change. At 1:00 a different backbeat is all that happens. For the ten seconds either side I checked the written guitars, bass, organ and kick, including lengths and accents: identical after shifting the timestamps. The hat falls from 24 hits to 16, the snare from 12 to 8. This is not a claim that two rendered takes are sample-identical.
The tell in the riff is two short pedal strokes into D-flat, then a late F. The opening picks out the ringing notes as guitar harmonics. At 0:40 the harmonium already breathes four times to the riff, ahead of the drummer. At 1:30 the guitars leave it the answer notes. A heavier second riff puts the chords just ahead of the feet. At 2:20 the drummer starts switching counts after four phrases, then two, then one. The open notes of the first riff come back as chords before the final D-flat, C, B-flat.

I kept an opening from which the band enters 6.0 LU louder, against 10.4 in the first full draft; it no longer leans over 1 dB to one side. This cost some recurrence score, especially on seed 11.
The bellows use the engine's pump on a dotted quarter, not a change of playback speed. Against the identical unpumped organ, the dip and recovery repeat each 625 ms. Unmastered, in stereo, the kept organ sits 9.3/9.4 dB under the band around the hinge (12.4/12.6 under in the lower, quieter draft), then 5.8 under when playing the answers exposed. Cost: at 250–500 Hz, two short windows at the hinge are 3.7/2.8 dB over the reference-record median in the mono sum. No master EQ used to hide it.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether the drummer changes the listener's footing or just seems to skip hits; whether the bellows let you hear the broad count in advance. No new card and no existing clip replaced.

note:
v2, THE NEXT FOOTFALL (palette, as drawn). The heavy riff at 1:50 gets ten seconds to itself. For the next four phrases, a low kettledrum answers its D-flat, F and C on the next broad beat. The guitar notes sit on sixteenths 3, 11 and 20 of the phrase; the mallet lands at 6, 12 and 24. It repeats the pitches, not the rhythm: the replies wait three, one and four sixteenths. Every fourth phrase the F folds down to C on both instruments. At 2:10 the guitars release the chords just before the drum hits, and they and the bass drop the last C entirely. That C is the drummer’s to land on the following downbeat. The last one opens the section at 2:20 where the drummer starts switching feet.

note:
v7, THE ORGAN TAKES THE OTHER WALK (whole-song draw). At 0:40 the drummer is still playing the quick six. The harmonium takes the riff’s four ringing notes, B-flat, D-flat, B-flat, F, and plays them on four broad steps. Two statements fit in five seconds. At 1:10, after the drummer has switched to the broad four, the organ remembers the quick six: the same four notes now fit three times into five seconds. Both phrases finish on F4, which becomes the lower voice of the held chord that follows. The existing organ does this instead of playing its old dyads in those two places; nobody else doubles it. The original demonstration across 1:00 is between the phrases and stays as written.
